SOURCE: "Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering", Gautier Izacard and Edouard Grave (Facebook AI Research, ENS, Inria). EACL 2021, pages 874–880 (arXiv 2007.01282). File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/izacard-2021-leveraging-passage-retrieval-generative-models.pdf

COVERAGE: Read all 25,716 of 25,716 extracted characters: body, Tables 1–2, Figure 3 axes and the full reference list. The paper has no appendix and no limitations section.

CLAIMS
- claim: Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) encodes each retrieved passage on its own, with the question prepended, then lets the decoder attend over all the encoded passages joined together. All evidence fusion happens in the decoder.
  number: none
  setup: T5 encoder-decoder. Each encoder input is formatted as "question:", "title:" and "context:"
  quote: "each retrieved passage and its title are concatenated with the question, and processed independently from other passages by the encoder... the decoder performs attention over the concatenation of the resulting representations of all the retrieved passages. The model thus performs evidence fusion in the decoder only"
  where: p.2 (876), §3 Reading
- claim: Encoding passages separately makes compute grow linearly with the number of passages, not quadratically. Joint decoding is what combines evidence across passages. This is how FiD differs from RAG (Lewis 2020b) and SpanSeqGen (Min 2020).
  number: none
  setup: an argument from the architecture. The paper measures no wall-clock time.
  quote: "computation time of the model grows linearly with the number of passages, instead of quadratically. On the other hand, processing passages jointly in the decoder allows to better aggregate evidence from multiple passages."
  where: p.2 (876), §3
- claim: Accuracy keeps rising as k grows from 10 to 100 passages. The authors cite other work saying extractive readers peak around 10–20 passages; they do not run those readers themselves.
  number: +6% TriviaQA, +3.5% NQ
  setup: FiD-base, validation sets. Training and test use the same k (Figure 3). The per-k values exist only as a plot.
  quote: "increasing the number of passages from 10 to 100 leads to 6% improvement on TriviaQA and 3.5% improvement on NaturalQuestions. On the other hand, the performance of most extractive models seems to peak around 10 to 20 passages (Wang et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019)."
  where: p.4 (878)
- claim: Per-k numbers from Table 2. Each row is the number of passages used in training, with testing always at 100 passages. Each pair is EM without and with a 1,000-step fine-tune on 100 passages.
  number: NQ 5→37.8/45.0, 10→42.3/45.3, 25→45.3/46.0, 50→45.7/46.0, 100→46.5. TriviaQA 5→58.1/64.2, 10→61.1/63.6, 25→63.2/64.2, 50→64.2/64.3, 100→64.7
  setup: dev sets, EM. The paper does not say whether this is the base or large model.

LIMITS:
- No experiments on passage order or position within the context. It gives no direct evidence for the "order" half of "Order and size of the context".
- The linear-compute claim is argued from the architecture and never measured. There are no inference latency or memory figures, and the decoder's cross-attention still covers all k×250 tokens.
- The "extractive readers peak at 10–20 passages" point is cited from other papers, not run here.
- Only short-answer factoid QA, scored with EM. There is no long-form generation and no measure of faithfulness or hallucination.
- The retriever is fixed and not trained jointly; the authors leave end-to-end training to future work. They also concede the need to "make this model more efficient... when scaling to large number of support passages".
- Dated: the reader is T5 at 770M parameters at most, from before long-context decoder LLMs. The comparison against GPT-3 is few-shot and closed-book.

BUILDS ON: T5 (Raffel et al., 2020); BART (Lewis et al., 2020a); DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); BM25 (Robertson et al., 1995); closed-book QA (Roberts et al., 2020); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020b); SpanSeqGen (Min et al., 2020); DrQA retrieve-then-read (Chen et al., 2017); REALM (Guu et al., 2020); ORQA and the experimental setting (Lee et al., 2019); FAISS.

CODE: none in the paper. The input format is quoted under the first claim.

FIGURES:
- Figure 1 (p.1): question plus retrieved passage, a seq2seq model, then the answer. It shows the two-component pipeline at a glance, which fits note 02's "The two components".
- Figure 2 (p.2): "Architecture of the Fusion-in-Decoder method." N encoders each read question + passage, their outputs are concatenated, and one decoder reads the result. It explains separate encoding with joint decoding faster than prose.
- Figure 3 (p.4): "Performance of Fusion-in-Decoder (base) on valid sets as a function of the number of retrieved passages." EM rises monotonically from 5 to 100 passages on NQ, TriviaQA and SQuAD. It is the clearest visual for the "size of the context" point.

PROBLEMS:
- The extraction is clean, and I found no embedded instructions.
- The figures came through only as axis ticks, so the per-k EM values in Figure 3 cannot be quoted. The quotable per-k numbers are in Table 2.
- The Table 1 header shows two TriviaQA columns without labels; the caption identifies them as open test and hidden test.
- The 44.1% BM25 figure in the text does not appear in any table.
